summary: Defines Uniform Resource Identifiers for referring to Domain Name System resources, so a DNS name, record class or type can be named in a URI. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A web-style address that points to an entry in the Internet's phone book instead of a web page.

subtitle: A dns: URI scheme for naming a piece of DNS data by its name, class and type.

tldr.problem: The DNS and URI-based protocols are separate worlds, so there was no standard way to refer to data stored in the DNS from a URI.
tldr.mechanism: The dns: scheme names a resource record set by domain name, with optional CLASS and TYPE query elements and an optional authority naming the server to ask.
tldr.outcome: Software such as security tools, DNS administration tools and programming packages can reference DNS data in a protocol-independent way, though the RFC does not expect wide implementation.

facts.label: Query elements
facts.value: CLASS and TYPE, each at most once

today: RFC 4501 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says it is not anticipated to be implemented widely.

sections.title: Introduction and Usage Model
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) translates host names into IP addresses, among other things. Many protocols use Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) to refer to data. RFC 4501 bridges the two by defining a URI scheme that can reference any data stored in the DNS.

The scheme focuses on the data, not the protocol. It has no way to set fields of the actual DNS protocol, so it can be used even where DNS is not spoken directly, such as in zone file editors and DNS-related configuration files. The RFC admits this does not cover every protocol parameter, and that a more detailed URI syntax may be needed for some applications. It is primarily meant to name DNS resources, but can also locate them for simple, common cases.
sections.eli5: It gives DNS entries an address you can write down and pass around, like a link, without caring how the entry is fetched.

sections.title: The dns: URI Syntax
sections.content:
A DNS URI designates a DNS resource record set, referenced by domain name, class, type and, optionally, the authority. It uses the generic syntax of RFC 3986, described in ABNF. Strings are not case sensitive, and free insertion of white space is not permitted.

The form is dns:, then an optional //authority/, then the dnsname, then an optional ? query. The query holds CLASS= and TYPE= elements separated by ;. Each of the two MUST NOT appear more than once, but they may come in either order. So dns:example?TYPE=A;TYPE=TXT is invalid, while dns:example?CLASS=IN;TYPE=A is valid.

Class and type may be a number or an IANA-registered mnemonic. Numbers MAY be used for newly introduced values, but SHOULD NOT be used for those defined in the DNS specification, and all implementations MUST recognize the mnemonics defined there.
sections.eli5: The address says which name you want, and optionally which kind of entry and which server to ask. The kind and class can be given in any order, but only once each.

sections.title: Defaults, Relative Names and Resolution
sections.content:
If the URI leaves things out, the authority is assumed to be locally known, the class is IN (Internet) and the type is A (Address). These defaults match the typical use of DNS: looking up addresses for host names.

Names not ending in . are taken as relative to the root, so dns:host.example and dns:host.example. both refer to host.example.. An empty name refers to the root.

To resolve a DNS URI with the DNS protocol, a client builds a query from the name, class and type. If an authority is given, that server receives the query; otherwise the default DNS server does. The RFC notes that DNS URIs could also be resolved by other means, such as multicast DNS, and do not require the DNS protocol. A client MAY check it understands the class and type before querying, but a proxy treating the answer as opaque data need not.
sections.eli5: If you do not say otherwise, it asks the usual question: what is the address for this name? Leaving the name empty means the very top of the DNS.

sections.title: Character Encoding and Escaping
sections.content:
Characters are encoded as in RFC 3986. The DNS protocol does not consider character sets, so the name is treated as an internationalized domain name (IDN) unaware slot.

Because . separates labels, a dot inside a label needs escaping, using the mechanism in section 5.1 of RFC 1035. The label exa.mple can be written exa\.mple, but URIs forbid a bare backslash, so it becomes %5c and the label is encoded exa%5c.mple. The same mechanism handles characters like ? and ;. Plain . and %2e are interchangeable in the name.

The scheme itself places no limit on which names can be encoded. Applications that restrict valid characters must make sure invalid ones do no harm.
sections.eli5: A dot normally separates the parts of a name, so a dot that is really part of a part needs a special disguise.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several examples. The URI dns:www.example.org.?clAsS=IN;tYpE=A names an absolute name with explicit class and type. Since IN and A are the defaults, dns:www.example.org identifies the same resource. A different type is requested with dns:simon.example.org?type=CERT.

An authority is given as in dns://192.168.1.1/ftp.example.org?type=A, which asks the server at 192.168.1.1 instead of the default one. Escaping is shown by dns:world%20wide%20web.example%5c.domain.org?TYPE=TXT, whose owner name contains spaces and a literal dot.
sections.eli5: Short links use the usual defaults; longer links spell out which kind of entry you want and which server to ask.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
A DNS URI that references the Internet DNS, and the data it points to, are public information. Within an internal DNS environment, the same handling rules as for that environment's DNS data apply. If the referenced data is used for security decisions, such as certificates stored in the DNS, implementations may need techniques like Secure DNS, CMS or OpenPGP to protect it in transit. The RFC leaves how to do this to the usage scenario.

Two covert-channel warnings are given. Accepting unknown query elements, such as ?secret=value, could let information leak, and so can small variations like upper and lower case in the name. The IANA has registered the dns URI scheme using the template in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The address is not secret, so if you trust the answer for something important you must protect it separately. Also, odd extra bits in an address could be used to sneak messages out.

data.title: dns: URI grammar
data.code:
dnsurl          = "dns:" [ "//" dnsauthority "/" ]
                  dnsname ["?" dnsquery]
dnsauthority    = host [ ":" port ]
dnsname         = *pchar
dnsquery        = dnsqueryelement [";" dnsquery]
dnsqueryelement = ( "CLASS=" dnsclassval ) / ( "TYPE=" dnstypeval )
